title: Chess is Art
reviewNotes: Montages, captions and complete native diagrams reviewed. Conditional final rook-mate pattern only, after White accepts the queen with Qxd3 at134 seconds. Native41 establishes the full fourteen-piece diagram: White Kg3/Qd3/Rg2/Bf2/Nd4/a2/b3/f4 against Kh7/Rh6/a7/f5/g4/g7; native42 confirms Rh3 mate. The f4 pawn came from the earlier capture and remains on the board. Native43 shows an animated rook while the source resets a variation, not a stable rook on h4 to splice into the game. Rh3# has an exact finite certificate ending in actual mate. The earlier fifteen-piece g4 position and White refusal Rh2/Qxf3+/Nxf3 remain outside this proof. A bounded twelve-ply strategy search from that larger root did not complete a certificate; source resignation or material gain is not treated as proof of those larger outcomes.
transcript: Chess is a form of art, as I've demonstrated to you with a lot of end game studies, but sometimes these incredible positions arise from real games, and that is what happened in the women's candidate tournament that just took place last week. Kateryna Lagno has the black pieces against her opponent Tan Zhongyi, and in this position Tan is pushing for an advantage having an extra bishop. Kateryna plays rook to F6, now attacking the queen and trying to get it out of the position, and Tan just picks up the free pawn on D5, but unfortunately, this is a blunder. But it is only a blunder because of an incredible and beautiful sequence that starts with the brilliant knight to F4. This is indeed a piece sacrifice despite black being already down a bishop. So, what's the idea? Well, of course, we're attacking the rook and the queen at the same time, so the knight cannot really be ignored. But if you try to create your own counter attack on the queen, now after rook to H6, you're actually getting checkmated by rook to H3, and the same thing happens if you try to move the queen away. Rook to H6 is going to lead to the same checkmate. So, Tan Zhongyi takes the knight. What's the big deal? Well, that knight was only sacrificed so that the rook could be open and go to H6 anyway. Well, of course, the queen is taking care of the back rank, but the king can just come to G3. But Kateryna continues with queen to D3 check. And this is when Tan Zhongyi probably realized that the position was actually hopeless for her because you cannot cover this check with the knight. After the pawn falls, you're just going to lose your queen, and you cannot move the king anywhere, so the check has to be blocked. And the queen goes to F3, but so what? What's the big deal? If we take the queen, the king is going to take back, and there's no checkmate, and sacrificing the rook to distract the king doesn't work because the queen is still defended. So, white seems to be simply out of the woods. How can black win here? Well, I'll show you how with the incredible G4, leaving the queen to hang. But of course, the queen is untouchable. If you take it, there is going to be a checkmate on H3 with only one rook left, but that's all it would take. So, the queen cannot be touched, but the white queen cannot move away. This is a pin. So, in the game, Tan Zhongyi played rook to H2 and lost the queen, and very soon after proceeded to lose the game. Follow me if you love incredible chess.
